items.title: A visit to author Amy Tan’s gorgeous Sausalito home
items.content:
Come with me to Amy Tan’s house for a brief moment, won’t you? We won’t be there long; just enough to time to sit down with the author of “The Joy Luck Club” and have a deeply enlightening chat that leaves you and me spiritually revived.

It’s not an arduous journey to Tan’s home. She lives just across the Golden Gate bridge in Sausalito, along a tight hillside road that feels a bit more LA than San Francisco. Tan and her husband Lou moved here after living in San Francisco proper for over 30 years. Here on a steep hillside overlooking the bay, the couple built a house that looks nothing like the custom-built McMansions the average celebrity is likely to erect in their own honor. The Tan home feels like a , all warm woods, open-air architecture, and an array of elaborate bird feeders to attract local species (Tan is a very, very avid birder). It’s also Americans with Disabilities Act compliant, elevator included, to accommodate for Tan’s physical limitations, including a type of epilepsy that leaves her unable to drive a car. This is a place where you’d feel welcome even if there was no one to greet you at the door.

But Amy Tan herself is here to greet us, and what a hostess she makes: seventy-four years old and sharp as hell, bright red lipstick, black leisurewear with a tasteful kimono over it, and a funky blue dye job for her signature bob haircut. She changes her hair color every so often, just because it’s fun. fun. Amy Tan is fun to hang with even when you’re talking with her about Lyme disease, or systemic racism, or any of the myriad topics that she and I discuss in the interview below, which has been edited and condensed for clarity. I hate to refer to it as an “interview,” because Tan is such an effortless conversationalist that one topic runs seamlessly into the next, and because she’s the sort of person who welcomes questions rather than dreads them. She sits down with me in the middle of her living room, and off we go.

Article continues below this ad

SFGATE: I love your house.

Thank you!We lived in San Francisco for 30 years. I said we need a place that’s going to be accessible. If I can’t walk, then I need to be able to just get into an elevator and go anywhere. You’ll see that all the outdoor spaces around here are level access. I can go out into the patio, go out on the veranda, and not feel trapped. That was the whole idea. Then it turned out this place is great for viewing birds because of all the windows.

SFGATE: Did you feel sad leaving San Francisco, or were you ready?

We did it gradually. We had a little pied-a-terre in Sausalito for five years before we decided to make Sausalito our home. We felt guilty to leave San Francisco, but I wanted a place where it was warmer. And I wanted a place where we could park. You come to Sausalito and you say, “Let’s go to a restaurant. Let’s go shopping,” and there’s parking. You go over to San Francisco, you’re going around and around. How many years of your life have you wasted going around trying to find a parking space?

Article continues below this ad

SFGATE: Oh I don’t even wanna think about it.

We also live part-time in New York. There’s subway, taxis. We’d never have a car there, either.

SFGATE: Where in New York?

Article continues below this ad

SoHo. We’ve been there for 30 years. We only bought in New York because my first editor, who was like a sister to me, had cancer in 1996, and she really wanted me there to help her. We rented a place that was way too expensive and way too big. Three bedrooms, two baths, wraparound penthouse. It was ridiculous in size.

SFGATE: That’s a nice apartment.

Then at the end of the year, my editor was still alive, surprisingly.

SFGATE: [laughs] You’re like, “What are you still doing here?”

Article continues below this ad

laughs] We just thought, we’re going to have to renew our lease, because otherwise she’s going to think  think she’s going to die. Then I said, “Why don’t we just buy a place?” Because it was cheaper than renting.

SFGATE: Do you still maintain a set writing schedule?

No, I haven’t had one that works for me since that bird book came out. The bird book was an unexpected book. It was not meant to be published. It was my editor’s idea.

Article continues below this ad

SFGATE: Did you like the book?

I love the book. I thought maybe it’d sell some small amount, because the birds here are not found on the East Coast or the Midwest. Why would people buy a book that doesn’t even have their species in it? It landed No. 1 on the New York Times bestseller list, then they ran out of stock six times! That kept me afloat during a political year. Because I just felt like I had to do things: pro bono events all over the place to raise money.

SFGATE: What kind of events?

A lot were birding events, but also events for Asian Pacific Fund or events for disabled, for conservation, all of those things. My husband and I started picking out charities that were affected by the new administration, and we just started donating.

Article continues below this ad

SFGATE: Were you doing any open activism to go with that?

Oh yes, of course. I even wore a sweatshirt that said, “I’m an American,” because in some people’s minds, it was doubtful that I was an American. I’m a birthright American. Meaning, I’m in the group of people Trump wanted to get rid of. He wants to get rid of our birthright citizenship. It was very distressing to think that there was a huge segment of people who supported that. It’s devastating to think they want to kick me out of the country. “We’ll get rid of these people who are not true Americans.”

SFGATE: I want to expand on that. With “The Joy Luck Club,” I feel like you were one of the most important figures in making the Asian American experience more well understood by this country’s mainstream. In the ensuing decades, particularly in this century, the Asian American influence on the greater culture has been far more prevalent and profound. Would that be accurate?

Article continues below this ad

In literature, definitely so. I was one back then. “Exotic.” I was afraid “The Joy Luck Club” would be perceived as this exotic species of book. I was surprised that it was taken a different way. I do have to say, however, that I don’t take credit for changing things much, because I wrote that book for myself. If I didn’t to help people understand Asian culture, I cannot be the one who then takes .

SFGATE: Also, the strain would show up in the work. It would be didactic.

SFGATE: What has it been like for you as an Asian American to watch this remarkable amount of progress culturally while, at the same time, we have the absolute revanchist bulls—t going on in the most powerful corridors of America? Do you feel optimistic? Crazy?

Article continues below this ad

I really struggled with people giving me the limelight early on. It was one book. No one book can satisfy that need [for Asian American representation]. But you can imagine how happy I am that we those books out there now. It’s all really good fiction. They’re winning the top prizes. They’re not seen as little adjuncts in literature anymore. In the early days, I was classified as Asian American literature.

SFGATE: There was probably a section that said exactly that at the bookstore.

Article continues below this ad

SFGATE: Like the “Asian” aisle of a grocery store.

Exactly. Yes, the specialty foods. The best was when my second book, “The Kitchen God’s Wife,” came out. It was found in the culinary section. That’s how people categorize books. It’s natural. But every review I got was by somebody who was Asian or in Asian academic fields in Asian history or politics or whatever. I was always reviewed from that lens.

SFGATE: Did you like that?

I hated it because I got Asian scholars who would say, “You haven’t presented a more enlightened view of Chinese culture. Your cultural norms seem to be taking place in the past with concubines and all of that.” I said, “You write from necessity and what propels you. My family history is actually in China. My grandmother was a concubine. She committed suicide as a result of that. My mother was in an arranged marriage, and had an abusive husband.” I said, “This is my life, and it’s what compels me to write fiction. I’m not going to write about Harvard-educated parents who belong to country clubs and all of that. That’s not the kind of story that compels me.”

Article continues below this ad

SFGATE: When’s the last time you went to China? Have you gone this century?

Oh, yes. Maybe eight years ago, but that’s a long time for me because I have family there. I need to see them because we’re all getting older.

SFGATE: Are you still writing fiction?

Article continues below this ad

Yes. This interview came in under the wire. I need to lock down, become more reclusive, and write. I have my novel started. I know where I want to go, but I need concentrated time when I’m alone. I also have this project I’m doing for the Monterey Jazz Festival with Joey Alexander that’s occupying a lot of my mind.

SFGATE: What’s the jazz project?

We’re going to be at Monterey Jazz Festival. I’m going to be reading excerpts from the book “The Backyard Bird Chronicles.” We’re going to pick birds and passages and things we’ll say. Then Joey is going to create the music for it. Neither of us is directing each other, but I wanted him to experience the birds so when he creates the music, he really knows who those birds are. I thought maybe he can feel he the bird. It doesn’t have to be just an attempt to represent bird song. It could be its bouncy behavior, its personality, its speed of movement. It could be his personal feelings about it. We don’t have to explain it. That’s part of the art. You don’t have to overexplain anything. You have to feel it.

SFGATE: How do you write? Are you a typewriter composer?

Article continues below this ad

Oh my God, no. I do write out ideas in a journal by hand. But when I write, I use a computer. I love the process of revision. Unfortunately or fortunately, a computer allows you to do as many revisions as you want until your editor says, “You’re done, you’re done, you’re done, stop.” I like that. I don’t want to let it go because once I do, it’s no longer mine. It’s out there.

SFGATE: I’ve always believed that a work of art is out there, readers have some agency over it, as in they have established their relationship with the work.

Yes, it’s a different book.

Article continues below this ad

SFGATE: You can go back like George Lucas and be like, “Oh, actually, this is my art now,” but that’s not how it works. Once you’ve created that relationship, it is what it is.

I’ve never had a review that captured what the book is for me. Never. That tells you how different it is, and I accept that.

SFGATE: It’s sort of beautiful in a way.

It is good because it is a very private endeavor. It’s in the moment. It’s a diary of me and what I’m thinking. My thoughts, my are in those books. Oftentimes, a page written on a particular day reflects something that that day. If I were to read it back, I’d know where I was and what I was thinking and feeling at that time. Nobody’s going to know that. Nobody has my life. It’s a different book for them, and that’s fine. Some people will find resonance in it, and some people won’t. The people who don’t will hate it, and that’s fine. I don’t read reviews anymore for that reason. I used to take them seriously and say, “Oh, my God, I have to have more role models in my fiction.” The only ones I’ve read, the bird book, I have read the reviews. They’re mostly positive. The ones that are negative say, “This is a book about birds.”

Article continues below this ad

SFGATE: “I thought it was going to be about robots.”

I know! People are weird about what they are looking for.

Article continues below this ad

SFGATE: Do you have a favorite bird right now?

The favorite changes all the time and for different reasons. Hummingbirds in the beginning were my favorite. They were so glamorous, the smallest bird in the yard. Then I went to the biggest bird in the yard, which is the great horned owl.

SFGATE: Do you have a least favorite bird?

Article continues below this ad

SFGATE: Well, do you have any you don’t like? Whenever I see a goose, I’m like, “F—k that goose.”

SFGATE: Wow. Now, are you just being polite?

Article continues below this ad

No. In fact, I am very clear about my distaste for people who call certain birds junk birds, trash birds.

SFGATE: Let me be clear. I just said, “F—k that goose.” I didn’t say it was a trash bird.

Well, [laughter] “F—k that goose” means you don’t want them there. I see the same birds day after day, and I never get tired of seeing them. That’s because there’s so much to learn about each of them. A lot of people don’t like pigeons. Pigeons are incredibly smart. They recognize faces. They descend from dinosaurs. In fact, their line of evolution comes from the T. rex!

SFGATE: OK, last thing. I wanted to ask about your fit. What is the jacket that you’re wearing?

Article continues below this ad

It’s an antique kimono. I have 20 of these things. I can go around wearing my sweat clothes, and then I can put this on and be ready.

SFGATE: And your necklace?

When my mother was 75, she had an 85-year-old boyfriend. We took them to Japan and China, and at the end, he bought this for me. It’s a lock that merchants used to use on their belts. They’re used to symbolize longevity. For children, it locks them to earth, only you usually have them much smaller in gold, 24-carat gold. That’s what this is. I get more compliments on this than anything. It probably cost $20 in China when we got it back in 1995.

SFGATE: And the blue is your natural hair color, I’m assuming. Yes?

Article continues below this ad

SFGATE: I love the hair color. It’s fantastic.

It changes. It was green last week.

Article continues below this ad

SFGATE: Do you have a set schedule for changing the dye?

No. When I see that it’s starting to fade into a different color, then I might change it. I do it myself. I just put different color on at different intensities, and then it’s always different, which I like.

items.title: Elizabeth Holmes' fiance is the worst man in America. Now we have him on tape.
items.content:
NOTE: This review contains spoilers for “You Can See Everything.”

Sometimes the best journalists are people who don’t even purport to be journalists. The late Anthony Bourdain was one such accidental herald, as was “Borat” star Sacha Baron Cohen before the gonzo comedian became recognizably famous no matter his alter ego. Let’s go ahead and add writer/performer Nathan Fielder to the list. You and I know Fielder best from “Nathan For You” and “The Rehearsal.” Everyone else is about to know him for “You Can See Everything,” a tag team effort with documentarian Lance Oppenheim that is not only the best film of 2026 so far, but also one of the finest works of journalism I’ve ever seen.

This movie arrives in theaters with plenty of deserved Oscar buzz. But in this case, a mere filmmaking award seems insufficient in recognition. As far as I’m concerned, this thing deserves a Pulitzer (categories be damned). And maybe a Nobel Prize.

Article continues below this ad

But I’m getting ahead of myself. In case you haven’t seen the film’s trailer, “You Can See Everything” is a portrait of infamous Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, who was convicted in 2022 of defrauding her company’s investors and is currently in prison in Texas. You can read all about Holmes in John Carreyrou’s book “Bad Blood,” an essential tick-tock of the Theranos scandal. The book not only tells the story of how Holmes led people to believe that her company’s revolutionary blood-testing hardware worked (it did not), but also of how the greater Silicon Valley culture inspired Holmes, and in some cases perhaps abetted her. The Theranos scandal was one of the highest profile financial scandals of this century, and Holmes was the haunting, unblinking face of it.

Holmes went dark for years after her malfeasance was exposed, until she and her fiance, Billy Evans, agreed to let Fielder and Oppenheim into their slipshod rental cottage in Del Mar for weeks on end and film the couple (and their two very cute children) as they prepared for Holmes to report to prison. Fielder and Oppenheim were allowed to film the Holmes family nearly 24/7, with Fielder at one point agreeing to stay with the family for an extended period of time. Hence, the film’s title. You will, indeed, see everything. Almost too much of everything, given that this doc runs nearly three hours, and given that the camera stays uncomfortably tight on its participants, Fielder included, for the bulk of that time.

You’ll also see Billy Evans’ penis, so be warned or titillated as you see fit.

Article continues below this ad

As Fielder ingratiates himself with Holmes and Evans, he gets them comfortable enough to ask the hard questions: about Theranos, about prison, and even about themselves. The resulting footage is often shocking. You will see Elizabeth Holmes, who still maintains she did nothing wrong, answer “no” when Fielder asks her if she’s ever lied in her life. You will hear Billy Evans, the real villain in this particular story, tell everyone in the room that he carries a gun on him 24/7. You will see Fielder screen the legendary “Who’s on first?” sketch for Holmes and her partner, with Holmes missing the central joke of the sketch entirely. You will see Fielder explain to Holmes that “Who” is the name of the guy on first base, with her still not really grasping it. And you’ll see Holmes’ partner tell her, “You see the world differently,” in a skin-crawling attempt to turn her seeming cluelessness into something laudatory. The Silicon Valley mindset at work.

Speaking of the Valley mindset, you will also see Holmes and Evans spend a great deal of time in this movie attempting to boot up Theranos 2.0. They even go so far as to drag out some of the original Theranos blood testing apparatus, which looks like a bunch of random parts from TigerDirect they hooked together, to show Fielder what their product can do. We do not see it doing anything on screen, but the couple assures that it would if it was, like, hooked up properly. 

These scenes are extremely funny, but funny isn’t what Fielder is looking for. He’s trying to figure out if this woman is a clueless naif, if she believes her own lies, or if she is playing the of an innocent woman, and doing so with such effectiveness that, to paraphrase Fielder, she might be the most manipulative person in the world.

Article continues below this ad

The answer proves fabulously elusive, and so Fielder and Oppenheim go to extremes in their attempt to find it. They hold the camera on Holmes’ rubbery elfin face for what feels like hours at a time, to see if she’ll blink (figuratively literally!). They interview Holmes’ visiting parents, with the father, former Enron exec Christian Holmes, casually telling Fielder that everything changed for his daughter “when she was raped.” To the furthest extreme, they bring in actress Amanda Seyfried — who  Holmes in the Hulu TV show “The Dropout” — to recreate any dialogues Fielder had with Holmes herself that couldn’t be recorded on camera. Seyfried is so convincing in mimicking Holmes that you, the audience, might forget which scenes were Seyfried talking to the camera and not Holmes herself. I know I did.

It gets crazier. After Holmes reports to prison, Seyfried joins Fielder on a trip to visit Billy Evans in a clandestine attempt to get Holmes’ partner to admit that, without Holmes’ knowledge, he demanded (and for a moment, received promise of), monetary compensation from the A24 studio for the couple’s participation in this documentary.

A brief pause here. Billy Evans is scion to the San Diego-based Evans Hotels family fortune. Evans met Holmes well after she’d become notorious, but tells Fielder early in “You Can See Everything” that he didn’t recognize her when the two first met. In fact, he fell in love with Holmes within an hour of meeting her, then found out who she was, still wanted to be with her anyway. Do you buy this story? Of course you don’t. This man is full of s—t, and that becomes even more apparent when he’s confronted by both Fielder and Seyfried after Holmes has reported to prison. That’s when we hear Evans sneer, “I’m better read than you,” at Seyfried — who, as a reminder, is one of the most skilled people in the world at her chosen profession. He also taunts Seyfried for getting “owned” on Twitter after she derided the late white supremacist Charlie Kirk, whom of course Evans actually admired. This man is an absolute piece of s—t.

Thankfully, Seyfried says as much, becoming audience surrogate after that alarming sequence and telling Fielder that Holmes’ partner is “bats—t crazy.” Amanda Seyfried might be the coolest person in Hollywood. As for Fielder, he’s left wondering if Holmes has been victimized by her own partner, by her former Theranos paramour Sunny Balwani (also now in prison, and whom Holmes also accused of raping her), and by God knows who else. Was this woman, once a billionaire, more pawn than mastermind? Fielder shows some (platonic) fondness for Holmes over the course of this film, but by this point in the story it’s hard to know if , the interviewer, is also playing a character in order to get what he wants.

Article continues below this ad

Fielder, to his credit, acknowledges the thorniness of all this. He’s openly uncertain of having Seyfried dramatize Holmes’ words on camera because, no matter how talented the actress is, it’s still not Holmes herself saying those words to the camera. He also doesn’t know if he’s surreptitiously fallen for Holmes’ graciousness, to the point where he questions himself to Seyfried for believing Holmes when she told him, almost on a lark, that she had no clue Evans was making money moves behind her back. That leads to Seyfried herself wondering if her own Hulu portrayal of Holmes was truth, blurred truth, or just fiction. By the end of the film, Seyfried isn’t sure what the word “fiction” should even mean.

That’s what makes this film a masterwork. “You Can See Everything” refers plainly to the extensive footage that Fielder and Oppenheim were able to obtain. But here’s a documentary that also shows you, the audience, its whole methodology. It allows you to see the potential flaws in its reporting, and how those flaws might impede the filmmakers’ attempt to find real answers. 

It’s that truly radical transparency that differentiates this documentary not only from the tacit sponcon docs that now plague your television (Billy Evans cites Prince Harry and Meghan Markle’s deal with Netflix as a reason that he should be paid by A24 for appearing on camera), but also from a lot of the best pure documentaries ever filmed. Here is a movie that exists on a level with Banksy’s “Exit Through the Gift Shop” as a superlative example of how the truth can be not just impossible to find but, with great determination, can be eradicated altogether. I’ll never forget it.
